title: Final Summary
text:
4 Answer to the research question
The answer is ambiguous because the question asks for a smallest value of (n), but the phrase “reasonably defensible as approximately normal” depends on several choices. It is not a property that switches on at one universal sample size.
First, the answer depends on the population being averaged. In this project, the current run uses seed 6599 and B = 10000 repetitions. The first stable passes were:

(n=75)

Cauchy
No stable pass through (n=500)



These results are evidence against treating (n=30) as a universal rule. For example, the Poisson population did pass at (n=30), with skewness about 0.142, excess kurtosis about -0.007, Q-Q correlation about 0.998, and Q-Q RMSE about 0.064. By contrast, the Exponential population still had skewness about 0.398 at (n=30), so it failed the same standard; it first passed at (n=100), where skewness was about 0.189. The rare-success binomial population passed at (n=50), not at the conventional rule-of-thumb value of 30.
Second, the answer depends on what “approximately normal” means. I made the judgment reproducible by requiring all four shape criteria—absolute skewness at most 0.20, absolute excess kurtosis at most 0.30, Q-Q correlation at least 0.995, and standardized Q-Q RMSE at most 0.08. I also required three consecutive passing candidate sizes. A researcher using a looser skewness threshold, a different Q-Q tolerance, or only visual inspection could select a smaller value. That does not necessarily mean one analysis is wrong; it means the analyses answer slightly different operational questions.
Third, “smallest” is relative to the sample sizes investigated. The simulation tested (n=2,5,10,15,20,30,40,50,75,100,150,200,300,500). Thus, for example, the reported (n=100) for the exponential population means the first stable passing value on this grid. It does not prove that every value between 75 and 100 fails. A finer search could refine the boundary.
Fourth, Monte Carlo results are estimates of the sampling distributions, not perfect observations of them. Changing the random seed changes the exact skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q measurements. That is why the project records the seed, uses 10,000 repetitions, and requires consecutive passes. The broad conclusions are more meaningful than the last decimal place.
Finally, the usual CLT assumptions matter. The Cauchy sample means did not produce a stable normal approximation through (n=500); at (n=500), the simulated skewness was about 87.46, excess kurtosis about 8213.51, and Q-Q correlation only about 0.093. The dependent process also failed at (n=500), with skewness about 0.282 even though its Q-Q correlation was about 0.998. A large nominal sample size does not automatically create a large amount of independent information.
Therefore, the most professional answer is: there is no single universal smallest sample size. For a specified population, diagnostic standard, simulation design, and purpose, the smallest defensible value is the first sample size whose evidence meets the stated standard. In this project, that value ranges from (n=2) to (n=100) for the finite-variance independent populations, while the dependent and Cauchy cases do not meet the standard within the investigated range.

title: Final Summary
text:
5 Population shape
Symmetry is associated with faster convergence in these experiments. The exponential, rare-success binomial, and two-component mixture cases retain right-skew or tail behavior longer. The Poisson case is also skewed, but its skewness is less extreme than the rare-success binomial case. These differences show why the population distribution matters when choosing a practical sample size.

title: Final Summary
text:
6 Assumptions and limitations
The Cauchy experiment is the exception to the finite-variance pattern: no stable sample-mean normality was found through (n=500), which is consistent with its lack of a finite mean and variance. The dependent process shows why nominal sample size can overstate the amount of independent information. The non-identical Bernoulli process shows that changing probabilities affect the variance calculation even when a bell-shaped average still develops.
The dependent machine-failure and mixture analyses use explicit models because the handout labels those population specifications as “coming soon.” If the instructor supplies official generators, those generator functions should be replaced while keeping the documented design and diagnostic rule unchanged.

title: Final Summary
text:
7 Reproducibility and seed sensitivity


Code
selected <- summary$smallest_n_judged_normal
selected <- selected[!is.na(selected)]
if (length(selected) > 0) {
  first_population <- names(studies)[which(!is.na(summary$smallest_n_judged_normal))[1]]
  n_for_check <- studies[[first_population]]$selected_n
  reproducibility_check(first_population, n = n_for_check,
                        seed_a = student_id, seed_b = 2026L, B = B)
}


  seed simulated_mean simulated_sd    skewness excess_kurtosis
1 6599    0.007620303    0.7085607 0.001796392      0.05137215
2 2026    0.010569596    0.7098162 0.008686944     -0.01669831


The exact simulated means, skewness, and kurtosis change when the seed changes. The conclusion is considered reproducible when the broad decision—such as “passes early,” “requires a large (n),” or “no stable (n) in the range”—does not change. The Cauchy case is expected to be the most seed-sensitive because its tails do not provide stable ordinary moments.

title: Final Summary
text:
8 Overall conclusion
The Central Limit Theorem describes an asymptotic tendency, not a universal sample-size switch. A responsible normal approximation requires attention to population shape, dependence, identical-distribution assumptions, tail behavior, and the purpose of the approximation. Monte Carlo simulation makes those differences visible and provides evidence for a population-specific judgment.

The observations are independent Uniform(0, 1) values. The population is bounded and symmetric but has a flat, non-normal shape. I expect symmetry to make convergence faster than for strongly right-skewed populations, although very small sample means will still show the bounded population’s shape.

title: Stress-Testing the Central Limit Theorem
text:
R / QUARTO · STATISTICAL COMPUTING · MONTE CARLO


What is the smallest sample size at which the sampling distribution of a sample mean is reasonably defensible as approximately normal?


This project treats that question as an empirical modeling problem. It applies one transparent decision rule across 11 populations, tests the result with numerical and graphical evidence, and documents where the usual CLT intuition breaks down.


The headline finding: there is no universal “n = 30” switch. The defensible threshold depends on population shape, dependence, tails, and the standard used to define “approximately normal.”

title: Stress-Testing the Central Limit Theorem
text:
1 The result in one minute
The same diagnostic screen produced thresholds from n = 2 for a standard normal population to n = 100 for an exponential population. The Cauchy and dependent-process cases did not meet the stability rule through n = 500. This range is the central result: sample size alone is not enough to justify a normal approximation.








Population
First stable pass
Evidence at the selected threshold




Standard normal
n = 2
Normality is preserved exactly under averaging.


Continuous uniform
n = 5
Symmetry supports fast convergence.


Six-sided die
n = 10
Discreteness smooths through averaging.


Poisson(1)
n = 30
Skewness ≈ 0.142; Q-Q correlation ≈ 0.998.


Exponential(1)
n = 100
Skewness falls to ≈ 0.189; at n = 30, it is ≈ 0.398.


Cauchy
None through 500
Skewness ≈ 87.46 and excess kurtosis ≈ 8213.51 at n = 500.



For the full comparison—including rare-success binomial, mixture, non-identical Bernoulli, and dependent-process results—see the final summary.

title: Stress-Testing the Central Limit Theorem
text:
2 What this project demonstrates


2.1 Experimental design
Each population is evaluated on the same candidate-n grid with B = 10,000 simulated sample means per candidate. The seed is reset before each experiment so every result can be reproduced independently.


2.2 Evidence-based judgment
“Approximately normal” is operationalized with skewness, excess kurtosis, normal Q-Q correlation, and standardized Q-Q RMSE. A threshold must pass at three consecutive candidate sizes.


2.3 Assumption awareness
The study deliberately includes skewed, discrete, heavy-tailed, dependent, non-identical, and mixture populations to test the limits of a rule-of-thumb rather than merely confirm it.

title: Stress-Testing the Central Limit Theorem
text:
3 Research question

What is the smallest sample size at which the sampling distribution of the sample mean is reasonably defensible as approximately normal?

There is no universal answer because “approximately normal” is not a binary population property. It depends on the population being averaged, the diagnostic thresholds, the candidate sample sizes, Monte Carlo variation, and whether the assumptions supporting the CLT are credible.
The professional answer is therefore population-specific: choose the smallest sample size whose numerical and graphical evidence meets a clearly stated standard. This project makes that judgment explicit rather than hiding it behind a single rule of thumb.

Read the AI log for the prompt record, validation steps, revisions, and remaining modeling assumptions.

title: Standard Normal Population
text:
1 Population and prediction
The observations are independent standard normal values, (X_i N(0,1)). The sample mean of normal observations is exactly normal for every positive sample size, so I expect the smallest investigated value, (n=2), to pass.

title: Standard Normal Population
text:
2 Experimental design and decision rule
For each candidate (n), I generated B = 10000 independent Monte Carlo samples and saved the mean of each sample. I investigated 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500. “Approximately normal” requires absolute skewness ≤ 0.20, absolute excess kurtosis ≤ 0.30, Q-Q correlation ≥ 0.995, and standardized Q-Q RMSE ≤ 0.08. I require three consecutive passing candidate sizes before selecting the first stable value.

title: Two-Component Mixture Population
text:
1 Population and prediction
This analysis uses a two-component mixture: 90% N(0, 1) and 10% N(5, 1). It is an explicit irregular, life/death-style substitute because the handout marks the official life/death population as “coming soon.” The population is asymmetric, with a separated minority component. I expect slower convergence than for symmetric populations, but eventual convergence because the mixture has finite mean and variance.

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Process
text:
Code
source("../R/helpers.R")

B <- B_DEFAULT

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Process
text:
1 Population and prediction
For a sample of size (n), the observations are independent Bernoulli values, but their probabilities change linearly from 0.50 to 0.90. They are therefore not identically distributed. The average success probability is 0.70. Because the observations remain bounded, I expect a bell shape eventually, although the usual iid explanation of the CLT does not apply directly.

title: Non-identical Bernoulli Process
text:
2 Experimental design and decision rule
I generated B = 10000 sample means at candidate sizes 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500. I use the same four criteria for approximate normality: absolute skewness ≤ 0.20, absolute excess kurtosis ≤ 0.30, Q-Q correlation ≥ 0.995, and standardized Q-Q RMSE ≤ 0.08. Three consecutive passes define a stable selection. The theoretical standard deviation uses the sum of the individual Bernoulli variances rather than an iid formula.

     main = paste("Non-identical means: n =", plot_n), xlab = "Sample mean")

      add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

The first stable pass is n = 75. This case separates identical distribution from independence: changing probabilities alter the variance and centering calculation, but the bounded independent contributions can still produce an approximately normal average.

title: Cauchy Population
text:
Code
source("../R/helpers.R")
student_id <- 6599L  # Replace with the last four digits of your student ID.
B <- B_DEFAULT
study <- study_population("cauchy", seed = student_id, B = B)
d <- study$diagnostics

title: Cauchy Population
text:
1 Population and prediction
The observations are independent Cauchy(location = 0, scale = 1) values. The Cauchy distribution has no finite population mean or variance, so the usual finite-variance Central Limit Theorem does not apply. I predict that ordinary sample means will remain unstable and will not meet the normality criteria.

title: Cauchy Population
text:
2 Experimental design and decision rule
I generated B = 10000 sample means at candidate sizes 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500. The common shape screen requires absolute skewness ≤ 0.20, absolute excess kurtosis ≤ 0.30, Q-Q correlation ≥ 0.995, and standardized Q-Q RMSE ≤ 0.08, with three consecutive passing values required. For Cauchy data, the simulated mean and standard deviation are reported descriptively only; they are not estimates of finite population parameters.

title: Cauchy Population
text:
4 Visual evidence


Code
plot_n <- max(N_VALUES)
x <- study$samples[[as.character(plot_n)]]
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(x, breaks = 50, probability = TRUE, col = "gray60", border = "white",
     main = paste("Cauchy sample means: n =", plot_n), xlab = "Sample mean")
qqnorm(x, main = paste("Normal Q-Q plot: n =", plot_n), pch = 16, cex = 0.3)
qqline(x, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)









Code
par(old_par)

title: Cauchy Population
text:
5 Conclusion
The first stable pass is no stable value in the investigated range. Within the investigated range, no stable (n) met all criteria. This is not evidence that a larger finite (n) must eventually work; it is evidence that ordinary sample means are not governed by the usual finite-mean, finite-variance CLT here. The heavy tails also make exact summaries highly seed-sensitive.
